newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Analysts sceptical of Japan Big Bang reforms.
newsitem.headline: Analysts sceptical of Japan Big Bang reforms.

text.p: Financial market analysts in Asia welcomed news on Tuesday that Japan planned to deregulate its financial markets in a five-year "Big Bang", but most said they would believe it when it happened.

"This may sound a little cynical, but we could have two or three more governments in Japan before 2001...therefore I'll believe it when I see it," the head of research at a European-based brokerage in Singapore said.
However, he added that a more flexible and liberal financial market in Tokyo could only benefit Asia as a whole.
"Any extra money attracted to Tokyo as a result of their Big Bang won't necessarily stay there. By osmosis some of the money will find a home elsewhere (in the region)," he said.

The move to deregulate Japan's financial markets has already been christened "Big Bang" -- the same epithet given to British financial market reforms in 1986 which removed a host of barriers within the industry.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto announced the main thrust of the scheme on Monday. Banks, securities houses and insurance companies will be able to enter each other's businesses while the products which they deal in can be expanded.
The measures will also cover such areas as the liberalisation of transaction fees and requirements for financial institutions to improve disclosure.

Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia, doubted local players were worried by the prospect of a deregulated Tokyo simply because many could not believe they would see it in their lifetimes.

"It's not just easing a few rules -- we're talking about a major cultural change which could take a generation or more," said Roberts. "It would take one hell of a bang to shake the culture of seniority and face-saving which dominates in Japan."
The country did have one major advantage, however, and that was money. "Their huge imbedded savings flow is the market's saving grace," he said.
Although the proposals were well-intentioned, Roberts said Japan needed to do more to address the most urgent concern of offshore investors.
"The overriding problem from an offshore point of view is not liberalisation but proper regulation of the domestic market, particularly on the recognition of bad debt," he said.

Because companies and banks were allowed to sweep bad debt under the carpet, financing costs were higher than for comparable offshore institutions. He said this was why Japan had to run an inappropriately lax monetary policy.
"A freer market is neither here nor there while that is not fixed," Roberts said.

Sriyan Pietersz, chief strategist of Capital Nomura Securities Plc in Bangkok, said: "There is no doubt that the Japanese liberalisation will affect Southeast Asian countries at some point over time."
Pietersz said Tokyo's deregulation would boost competition among players in Japanese financial and equity markets, leading to a gradual increase in funds flowing out of Japan.
"It will boost competition, squeeze returns which will become thinner and encourage more, but gradual, outward flows of funds to other regional markets," he said.

Roger Kerr, economist and commentator at Bancorp Treasury Services Ltd in New Zealand, said of the move: "It can only be positive that other Asian economies open their financial markets up and get them more developed as well.
"Deregulation in New Zealand has made it a very competitive place and (a) good deal for users of financial markets. That's been our experience," he said.
